Photoredox/Copper Dual-Catalyzed Regioselective 1,4-
Arylcyanation of 1,3-Enynes for Multifunctionalized Allenyl Nitriles
Qilong Wu, Xufeng Li, Jian Lv, Yongjia Shi, and Daoshan Yang*

ABSTRACT: A copper/photoredox dual-catalysis-enabled 1,4-arylcyanation of 1,3-enynes to afford tetrasubstituted allenyl nitriles
was initially developed. The reaction features good reaction generality and high reaction regioselectivity, providing facile access to
multifunctionalized allenyl nitriles. This strategy achieves the construction of aryl-containing tetrasubstituted allenyl nitriles via
indirect arene C−H functionalization. It also serves as an important complement to thianthrenium salt chemistry.
A
s an important class of molecules, allenes find widespread
applications in natural products and pharmaceuticals
(Scheme 1a).
1
Additionally, they play crucial roles in synthetic
chemistry and drug design.
2
Therefore, chemists have been
making persistent efforts to synthesize functionalized allenes
including nucleophilic substitutions,
3
prototropic isomerization
of alkynes,
4
sigmatropic rearrangement of propargylic mole-
cules,
5
and other elegant methods.
6
Despite the success of
these methods, the unavailability of prefunctionalized starting
materials has limited their wide applications. In recent years,
conjugated 1,3-enynes have increasingly been considered as
key synthons for creating multisubstituted allenes, which is
achieved through 1,4-addition to bring in two functional
groups at the same time.
7
In this context, transition-metal-
catalyzed 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes through allenyl
ionic intermediates is well developed (Scheme 1b).
8
Radical-
induced 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes can generate
highly reactive and unusual short-lived allenyl radical
intermediates, which can easily form allenyl cations or allenyl
anions through oxidation or reduction pathways. In this regard,
1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes using a metallic radical
catalysis strategy has emerged as a reliable robust approach
toward functionalized allenes.
9
Very recently, a number of
elegant synthetic methods have been developed by Ma,
10
Wu,
11
Liu,
12
Bao,
13
and other groups.
14
In these reactions,
allenyl radicals were obtained via radical addition to the C�C
double bond in 1,3-enynes and subsequent isomerization. The
reactive allyl radicals reacted with the metal-FG (functional
group) species, generating metal-allenyl intermediates that
underwent reductive elimination to give the allenes (Scheme
1c). Although impressive success and breakthroughs have been
achieved in this field, there are still challenges in controlling
the regio- and chemoselectivities of multicomponent catalytic
systems through the free radical approaches.
Organic reactions promoted by visible light are regarded as
some of the best green methods.
15
Very recently, significant
progress has been made in the synthesis of multifunctionalized
allenyl nitriles through free radical 1,4-difunctionalization of
1,3-alkynals under photoredox/transition metal catalysis
conditions. In these works, the radical precursors are mainly
limited to C
sp
3
sources (Scheme 1d).
16
Literature surveys
indicated that 1,4-arylcyanation of 1,3-enynes to afford
tetrasubstituted allenyl nitriles has not been reported thus
far. The reason might be the lack of appropriate sources of aryl
radicals and effective catalytic systems. Recently, thianthrenium
salts have been widely employed as aryl radical precursors in
diverse organic transformations.
17
Based on the excellent work
reported previously and the continuous interest of our group in
photocatalytic radical reactions,
18
we hypothesize that merging
visible light photoredox catalysis and transition metal catalysis
might offer a general strategy for synthesizing multifunction-
alized allenyl nitriles through radical-type 1,4-difunctionaliza-
tion of 1,3-enynes (Scheme 1e).

At the outset of our investigation, 1,3-enyne 2a, aryl
thianthrenium salt 1a, and TMSCN were chosen as the model
substrates to optimize the reaction conditions, including the
ligands, solvents, catalysts, bases, and photoredox catalysts. As
shown in Table 1, after a series of systematic screenings of
reaction parameters, a 1,4-arylcyanation reaction was achieved
to deliver the expected multifunctionalized allenyl nitrile 3a in
68% yield using photoredox/copper dual catalytic systems
(entry 1). Results of our experiments revealed that other
nitrogen ligands led to decreased yields of 3a (entry 2, see the
SI for more details). Replacing DMSO with other solvents,
including MeCN and DMA, was less efficient (entry 3, see the

After obtaining the optimum reaction conditions, we
investigate the synthetic potential of this photoredox/copper-
catalyzed strategy for the synthesis of tetrasubstituted allenyl
nitriles (Scheme 2). First, various aryl thianthrenium salts were
examined, and either electron-donating or electron-with-
drawing groups on the aromatic ring were all compatible
with this protocol, giving the desired products in moderate to
good yield (3a−3i). The structures of the products can be
confirmed through single-crystal X-ray diffraction (3g).
Additionally, the heterocycle-containing aryl thianthrenium
salts smoothly converted to the corresponding products in
moderate yields (3h and 3i). A series of functional groups,
including methoxyl, ester, cyano, a C−Cl bond, and a C−Br
bond, were tolerated, which could afford an opportunity for
further modifications. Unfortunately, using alkenyl or alkyl
thianthrenium salts could not provide the corresponding
products (see SI for more details). Next, we turned our

We carried out a gram-scale reaction to demonstrate the
synthetic applicability of our method. As shown in Scheme 3a,
the reaction proceeded smoothly and gave 3a in 70% isolated
yield under irradiation of two 390 nm LEDs (15 W), thereby
indicating that this photochemical protocol is easy to scale up.
To further demonstrate the practicability of the current
method, the derivatization transformations of the obtained
allenyl nitriles were conducted. As shown in Scheme 3b, the
cyano group in product 3c could be transferred to the aldehyde
group at −78 °C with 3 equiv of DIBAL-H. Additionally,
treatment of 3n with phenylacetylene 7 provided the coupling
product 8 in 60% yield through a palladium-catalyzed
Sonogashira coupling reaction.
To gain an understanding of the mechanism, a series of
control experiments were conducted. As shown in Scheme 4a,
the model reaction was completely inhibited by adding 3.0
equiv of the radical scavenger (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-

detected by HRMS analysis. These results indicated that the
aryl radical might be the key species in the current conversion

mechanism is depicted in Scheme 5. Excitation of photo-
catalyst PTH A leads to the active state B, which undergoes
single electron transfer with the aryl thianthrenium salts 1 to
produce the corresponding aryl radical D. Subsequently, the
aryl radical adds to 1,3-enyne to form propargyl radical E, and
its resonance structure is allenyl radical F. Subsequently, the

In conclusion, we have successfully demonstrated the first
photoredox/copper dual-catalysis-promoted 1,4-arylcyanation
of 1,3-enynes for the synthesis of multifunctionalized allenyl
nitriles using thianthrenium salts as aryl radical precursors. The
reaction features exceptional regio- and chemoselectivities,
mild reaction conditions, and broad functional-group tolerance
and provides an efficient route to the synthesis of aryl-
containing allenyl nitriles in a single step. Mechanistic studies
indicate that aryl thianthrenium salts serve as aryl radical
precursors and will inspire new opportunities for the design of
radical-mediated multicomponent reactions. Further applica-
tions of this method and the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of
optically active allenyl nitriles are currently underway.

In conclusion, we have successfully demonstrated the first
photoredox/copper dual-catalysis-promoted 1,4-arylcyanation
of 1,3-enynes for the synthesis of multifunctionalized allenyl
nitriles using thianthrenium salts as aryl radical precursors. The
reaction features exceptional regio- and chemoselectivities,
mild reaction conditions, and broad functional-group tolerance
and provides an eficient route to the synthesis of aryl-
containing allenyl nitriles in a single step. Mechanistic studies
indicate that aryl thianthrenium salts serve as aryl radical
precursors and will inspire new opportunities for the design of
radical-mediated multicomponent reactions. Further applica-
tions of this method and the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of
optically active allenyl nitriles are currently underway.
